evidence.label: family statement carried by police

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend the sample’s focus on search developments because an accurate appeal and clear explanation of confirmed information can serve a missing-person investigation. We report what a search specialist said as his account, not as a police conclusion.

As the search continued, rumor and unofficial activity became part of the public-interest story. We would attribute claims, state what police confirmed, and avoid presenting online speculation as fact.

When police disclosed sensitive information, scrutiny of necessity and proportionality became legitimate. We would explain the stated reason for disclosure without repeating private details beyond what readers need.

This sample has four Sky headlines and is not a census. We would link the primary statements and distinguish the later review announcement from a final finding. We would also avoid language suggesting that a specialist’s view settled the search or that public curiosity justified disclosing private information. Our account should make clear who said what, when it was said, and what authorities had confirmed at that point. Those distinctions let readers assess urgency without treating speculation as fact. We would not treat prominence as proof of accuracy.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting the search, the public handling of information and later oversight because each raised questions of public importance. Our sample includes dated headlines from a short, intense period, not all coverage.
We would distinguish a specialist’s account, police statements and independently established facts. A working hypothesis is not proof, and online speculation should not be elevated into evidence.

After police disclosed sensitive personal information, the story required scrutiny of necessity, privacy and proportionality. Once the family asked for privacy after recovery, care should govern what detail remains relevant.

The sample contains four a publisher rows and is incomplete. We would link official records, avoid implying that an announced inquiry is a finding, and state clearly what the headlines do not tell us. We would also explain that the family’s request for privacy changes what a proportionate follow-up looks like. New oversight can justify reporting, but an announced review is not a final answer. Our defence is strongest when readers can see the uncertainty and the limits of each source. We would distinguish the question that was asked from the conclusion any later review reached.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting the search and its accountability questions, including the difference between official information and claims by private searchers. Our three headlines are selected examples, not a complete record.

We would attribute allegations and explain when police confirm or correct information. A private specialist’s view should not be described as a police finding; later reviews must be dated and their status stated.

Coverage can inform the public while also increasing intrusion. Sensitive personal details should be reported only when necessary to explain a decision or accountability question, with the family’s privacy respected.

The sample is event-led and limited to three a publisher headlines. We would link statements and judgments, and avoid asserting that a review announcement itself resolved the questions it was set up to examine. We would also avoid repeating sensitive information merely because it is available. Public accountability can be served by explaining why a disclosure occurred and what oversight followed, without turning private circumstances into a recurring headline hook. Our short sample cannot tell readers whether every article met that standard. We would also make clear that none of the selected headlines represents the family’s full experience.

scrutinyCriteria.label: Fair context
scrutinyCriteria.question: Were allegations, responses and unresolved findings represented fairly?

scrutinyCriteria.label: Framing & power
scrutinyCriteria.question: Did the coverage invite scrutiny or stereotyping, ridicule and superiority?

scrutinyCriteria.label: Care & persistence
scrutinyCriteria.question: Was continued attention proportionate after distress or vulnerability became known?

scrutinyCriteria.label: Comparable treatment
scrutinyCriteria.question: Would the outlet apply the same intensity to a genuinely comparable case?

scrutinyCriteria.label: Transparency

publicContext.intro: Nicola Bulley disappeared in Lancashire in January 2023. A search, public speculation, police disclosures and criticism of intrusive coverage unfolded over the following weeks. She was found dead on 19 February. Ask when useful search information gave way to speculation or intrusion, and whose decisions warranted scrutiny.
publicContext.allegationResponse: Her family’s requests for privacy matter to the assessment. Later official reviews are identified as retrospective; this game does not attribute her death to reporting.

sequence.text: A private search specialist said his team had not located Bulley in a specified section of river.
Police said two people had been arrested on suspicion of malicious communications as rumors and in-person searching drew attention.
Police disclosed a high-risk classification and sensitive personal information at a press conference, saying they were addressing speculation.
A body was found; later identification confirmed it was Nicola Bulley, and family requested privacy.
The College of Policing review and IOPC inquiry were announced.
